repeal

/rih-PEEL/ — rhymes with squeal · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To repeal a law or policy is to officially cancel it through an act of a lawmaking body, ending its legal effect.

Lawmakers voted to repeal the outdated curfew law.

Worked Example

After mounting public outcry over its unfairness, Congress moved to repeal the decades-old tax that had burdened small businesses.

The word repeal is precise here because it captures the formal, official process of erasing a law's legal effect entirely—not just modifying one part, but voiding the whole law. 'Cancel' is too vague; repeal specifically means ending legislation with legal power.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

cancel: Cancel is the everyday word for calling something off — a trip, an order, a subscription — and it needs no special authority. Repeal is cancellation with legal machinery behind it: a lawmaking body votes to end a law's legal effect, something no ordinary person can do.

reverse: Reverse means to change a decision to its opposite, so the outcome now points the other way. Repeal does not flip a law into its opposite — it wipes the law off the books entirely, leaving nothing in its place unless lawmakers write something new.

revoke: Revoke means an authority takes back something it granted — a license, a permit, a privilege — usually from one person or group. Repeal aims at the law itself: a legislature cancels the rule for everyone, not just for one holder of it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enact: to officially make a proposal into law

ratify: to formally approve and make officially valid

Where it sits · how completely the law is undone — modify → amend → overturn → repeal

modify vs. repeal: To modify a law is far milder than to repeal it — modifying makes small adjustments, while repeal wipes the law off the books entirely.

amend vs. repeal: Amend is stronger than modify but still weaker than repeal: an amendment formally rewrites parts of a law, while repeal cancels the whole thing.

overturn vs. repeal: Overturn comes close to repeal — a court can overturn a ruling and undo its effect — but repeal is the fullest step, officially erasing a law's legal force for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back (Latin (via Old French))

Root — peal (from apeler)

Root — peal (from apeler): to call (Old French, from Latin appellare)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- means 'back' and the root means 'to call,' so repeal literally means 'to call back.' When lawmakers repeal a law, they call it back — officially canceling it and ending its legal effect.

Use the root in a new word: appeal

Use the root in a new word: appeal: When you appeal a referee's decision, you call on a higher authority to reconsider it — the same 'call' root that hides inside repeal.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal

Repeal is the formal, legal term—reach for it when discussing the official cancellation of laws or policies. For canceling dinner plans or removing an item from a menu, use the plainer 'cancel.'
